# Homogeneous cap-moment costs and exact cone-gradient collapse

This note classifies a bounded family of scalar cap objectives and
normalizations. The source is fixed. The conclusions are first-order
statements at vertex-isolating simplex caps; they do not resolve OC or
exclude possible information from caps meeting several fibers.

## 1. Three cap moments and their exact differentials

Let the source have positive full-dimensional continuous fibers in R^d,
`d>=1`. A cap has nonzero continuous normal and affine margin

`L(z,x)=a dot z+u dot x-b`.

Write

`c=int 1_(L>=0) dmu`, `Psi=int L_+ dmu`, `T=int L_+^2 dmu`.

For an affine margin variation `dot L`, the first moments have exact
derivatives

`dot Psi=int_(L>=0) dot L dmu`,
`dot T=2 int_(L>=0) L dot L dmu`.                       (1)

At a regular cap,

`dot c=int_(L=0) dot L d tau`,
`d tau=dH_(d-1)/|u|` on each fiber section.             (2)

For polytope supporting-facet limits, (2) has the previously proved
Clarke interpretation with one consistent effective density in `[0,1]`.
The formulas in (1) are continuously differentiable even at those
contacts, since the cap boundary has zero d-volume and its margin is
zero. No ambient `(n+d)`-dimensional volume is used.

Consequently a smooth scalar cost `Phi(c,Psi,T)` has the affine-moment
gradient of the generally SIGNED measure

`Phi_c tau + Phi_Psi mu|H + 2 Phi_T L mu|H`.             (3)

Positivity of `Phi` does not make all three coefficients nonnegative.
One cannot silently regard (3) as a positive transport source.

Under an allowed invertible continuous affine transformation and an
integer unimodular transformation, writing the same margin in the new
coordinates multiplies each of `c,Psi,T` by the common fiber Jacobian
`Delta`. Multiplying the margin itself by `s>0` instead gives

`(c,Psi,T) -> (c,s Psi,s^2 T)`.                         (4)

These two operations are distinct. Ratios such as `cT/Psi^2` are
invariant under both. A source-homogeneous expression of degree h can
be made invariant under the Jacobian by dividing it by `M^h`.

## 2. Every vertex-isolating simplex cap has the same moment ratios

Suppose the cap has positive volume in exactly one simplex fiber and
is strictly empty on all other fibers. In that simplex it contains
exactly one strictly positive-margin vertex `v`, and every other vertex
has strictly negative margin. Put `H=L(z,v)>0`. The captured set is a
d-simplex with apex `v` and base in `L=0`. Homothety about the apex
gives, for `0<=s<=H`,

`mu{L>=s}=c(1-s/H)^d`.

Therefore its conditional margin has density
`d(1-s/H)^(d-1)/H`, and for every real `p>-1`,

`int_H L^p dmu
   =c H^p Gamma(p+1)Gamma(d+1)/Gamma(d+p+1)`.           (5)

In particular,

`Psi=cH/(d+1)`, `T=2cH^2/[(d+1)(d+2)]`,
`R:=cT/Psi^2=2(d+1)/(d+2)=:kappa_d`.                  (6)

All strict vertex-margin signs persist in an open parameter
neighborhood. Thus `R` is identically constant on that neighborhood,
and its full gradient, not just its radial derivative, vanishes there.
Every smooth function of `R` has the same property. This is an exact
local identity, not a limiting or numerical equality case.

More generally put

`phi(c,H)=Phi(c,cH/(d+1),2cH^2/[(d+1)(d+2)])`.

On the open cone-cap parameter region,

`D Phi=phi_c D c+phi_H D H`,                            (7)

where

`phi_c=Phi_c+H Phi_Psi/(d+1)
                +2H^2 Phi_T/[(d+1)(d+2)]`,
`phi_H=c Phi_Psi/(d+1)
                +4cH Phi_T/[(d+1)(d+2)]`.

Here `D c` is the section feature and `D H=(z,v,-1)` is the apex
feature in `(a,u,b)` coordinates. Thus all the apparently different
interior positive-moment gradients collapse to two geometric features.

## 3. Complete classification under two homogeneities

Assume `Phi` is homogeneous of source degree h and margin degree k:

`Phi(Delta c,Delta Psi,Delta T)=Delta^h Phi(c,Psi,T)`,
`Phi(c,s Psi,s^2 T)=s^k Phi(c,Psi,T)`.

For `c,Psi>0`, every such function has exactly the form

`Phi(c,Psi,T)=c^(h-k) Psi^k f(cT/Psi^2)`.               (8)

Indeed first scale c to one and then scale the mean margin `Psi/c`
to one. Conversely (8) has both homogeneities. No rationality or
integrality of h or k is required on this positive domain.

Combining (6)--(8), on every strict cone cap,

`Phi=f(kappa_d)c^h[H/(d+1)]^k`,
`D Phi=(h Phi/c)D c+(k Phi/H)D H`.                     (9)

This gives the following exact alternatives.

* If `k=0`, the gradient contains only the cap-mass/section feature.
* If `h=k=0`, it vanishes identically throughout the open cone region.
* If `k Phi!=0`, a nonzero apex feature remains, with coefficient
  `k Phi/H`.
* If `f(kappa_d)=0`, the cost and all its affine-margin derivatives
  vanish on this cone region, regardless of h and k.

In particular a margin-scale-invariant, source-degree-one cost is
`c f(R)`, and its gradient on a cone is merely `f(kappa_d)D c`.
It may have additional behavior off the cone region, but at these
sharp caps it carries no new interior first-moment feature.

## 4. Nonzero margin degree retains the same metric abnormality

Fix a positive definite matrix A and normalize continuous normals by
`u^T A u=1`. Consider a canonical centroid vertex cap in an isolated
simplex fiber, with fiber centroid g and apex v. Its own section
centroid is g and `H=u dot(v-g)>0`.

In a cap-cover stress, suppose the contact for this cap is g and the
multiplied other-fiber section terms vanish. These hypotheses hold
at the binary sharp-simplex covers considered below. Equation (9),
the budget derivative, and the mass equation remove every own-section
term from the continuous equation. With objective multiplier
`alpha_0`, what remains is

`alpha_0 (k Phi/H)(v-g)+sigma A u=0`.

Homogeneous Euler differentiation of the full affine margin fixes
`sigma=-alpha_0 k Phi`. Therefore, if `alpha_0 k Phi!=0`,

`v-g=H A u`.                                          (10)

This is precisely the same geometric condition as for the hinge.
For all cap types of a simplex it is equivalent to A being a positive
scalar multiple of that simplex's covariance, as proved in
`candidate a5bd7e36a76479fe`.
Changing h, k, or the shape-ratio factor cannot alter (10).

In contrast, when `k=0` and `h Phi>0`, the pure section derivative
does admit a normal canonical stress with zero budget multipliers in
any fixed quadratic metric. Use local circuit weights proportional
to the effective coarea masses `S_i=d c/H_i`. They balance because
`sum_i S_i u_i=(d+1)c sum_i beta_i=0`. Their section centroids and
contacts are the same point g. The coverage multiplier is
`(h Phi/c)sum_i S_i`, and the sphere multipliers are zero. This
eliminates the abnormality, but the retained objective gradient is
exactly a mass/section gradient.

In particular take the actual two-fiber body with
`K_0=conv(0,e_1,e_2)` and `K_1=diag(2,1/2)K_0`, and take A to be its
residual covariance `(1/144)[[20,-4],[-4,5]]`. At the minimum feasible
cap budget `2/9` and six caps, the canonical cap classification and
unique own-centroid contacts are unchanged by this choice of objective.
For every smooth homogeneous cost with `k!=0` and
`f(kappa_2)!=0`, no positive-objective-multiplier stress is possible.
The canonical condition (10) fails for the first fiber's e_1 cap.

Supporting coincidences on the other fiber do not invalidate this
conclusion. In the total derivative, an other-fiber section has
coefficient `alpha_0 Phi_c+r`, whereas the own-fiber derivative is
the decomposition (9) plus the budget term. The binary base equation
forces the multiplied other-fiber section contribution to vanish.
This argument does not require that its coefficient be positive.
After that elimination, (10) follows exactly as above.

This is a local stress obstruction at the sharp cover class. No
existence theorem for global minimizers of an arbitrary cost (8),
especially at zero cap moments, is asserted.

## 5. Scalar moment normalization cancels the apex term instead

Now remove the external quadratic normalization. Let a positive smooth
scalar normalization `N(c,Psi,T)=1` have source degree h_N and nonzero
margin degree k_N. Let a cost F have corresponding degrees h_F,k_F.
Suppose both ratio factors `f_N(kappa_d)` and `f_F(kappa_d)` are
positive. On a cone, the normalization is regular since

`partial_H N=k_N N/H!=0`.

For source-Jacobian invariance one may instead impose
`N/M^(h_N)=1` and use objective `F/M^(h_F)`. The source and M are
fixed in this variation, so this changes only constant prefactors
below, not the exponent or the gradient classification.

Solving it gives

`H/(d+1)=f_N(kappa_d)^(-1/k_N)c^(-h_N/k_N)`.

The exact reduced cost on this constraint is therefore

`F_eff(c)=f_F(kappa_d) f_N(kappa_d)^(-k_F/k_N)c^rho`,
`rho=h_F-k_F h_N/k_N`.                                (11)

This also describes its stress directly. If the normalization
multiplier is sigma, cancellation of the apex feature requires

`sigma=-k_F F/(k_N N)`.

The remaining own-section coefficient is exactly
`F_eff'(c)=rho F_eff(c)/c`. Thus scalar moment normalization removes
the metric obstruction by reducing the cone's first-order objective
to a power of its mass. It does not leave an additional independent
interior first-moment feature there.

For strictly isolated canonical simplex caps, if `rho>0`, this supplies
a normal stress with zero budget multipliers for arbitrary simplex
shapes. Within each fiber all canonical cap masses agree, so (11)
gives the same positive section coefficient for each type. Their
normalized apex heights also agree. The effective coarea masses are
`d c/H`, hence equal, and the normalized normals are a common multiple
of the barycentric gradients. Use uniform local circuit weights and
coverage multiplier `(d+1)F_eff'(c)d c/H`; section centroids equal the
contact g, so every equation holds after the apex cancellation.
If `rho=0`, even this remaining derivative vanishes. These statements
are normal-stress constructions, not global minimality claims.

Examples make the distinction explicit.

1. With `N=Psi/c=1` and `F=Psi`, the reduced objective is exactly c
   for every cap, not only for cone caps.
2. With `N=sqrt(T/c)=1` and `F=Psi`, the cone objective is
   `c/sqrt(kappa_d)`. Equivalently, before fixing scale, it is the
   margin-invariant cost `c/sqrt(R)`. Its cone derivative is only a
   constant multiple of `D c`.
3. A normalization depending only on `R` has zero gradient on every
   strict cone cap and cannot fix margin scale there. A normalization
   of margin degree zero likewise leaves the scaling freedom intact;
   by itself it cannot prevent a positive-margin-degree objective
   from approaching zero under margin shrinkage.

The same collapse holds for any finite collection of positive cap
moments: formula (5) expresses them all in terms of c and H on a cone.
Scale-invariant combinations eliminate H; regular scalar
normalizations determine H from c. The classification here does not
assert a corresponding collapse for a general cap intersecting
several fibers or for a nonconical continuous cap.
